answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Voltaire’s letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia, dated 28 November 1770. The familiar English wording is S. G. Tallentyre’s translation in Voltaire in His Letters (1919); the French reads “Le doute n’est pas un état bien agréable, mais l’assurance est un état ridicule.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia
“Le doute n’est pas un état bien agréable, mais l’assurance est un état ridicule.”
S. G. Tallentyre, Voltaire in His Letters (G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1919), p. 232

source.excerpt: Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is an absurd one. What is most repellent in the System of Nature — after the recipe for making eels from flour — is the audacity with which it decides that there is no God, without even having tried to prove the impossibility.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its Sourced section, dated 28 November 1770, with the French original — not among the misattributed or disputed quotes.
The full sentence, with the swipe at d’Holbach’s System of Nature, is preserved in S. G. Tallentyre’s 1919 translation and traced to p. 232 of Voltaire in His Letters.
French sources reproduce the same passage from Voltaire’s Correspondance (1770), confirming “l’assurance est un état ridicule” as the original.
source.excerptNote: Tallentyre’s 1919 English rendering. Voltaire is attacking the dogmatic atheism of d’Holbach’s Système de la nature (1770): his target is not belief but certainty of any kind.
source.rightsNote: Voltaire’s French letter dates to 1770 and the standard English wording is S. G. Tallentyre’s translation first published in 1919 — both well before 1931 — so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: François-Marie Arouet, known by his pen name Voltaire, was a leading figure of the French Enlightenment, celebrated for his wit, his campaigns against religious dogmatism and intolerance, and works such as Candide and the Philosophical Dictionary. In his later years at Ferney he carried on a vast correspondence, and this line comes from a 1770 letter attacking the atheism of d’Holbach’s Système de la nature — a plea for humility against those who claim total certainty.

misattribution.heading: The wrinkles
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Voltaire is sound, but two details are routinely garbled online.

items.why: Countless sites cite a letter to Frederick II dated 6 April 1767. Wikiquote’s Talk page documents that the real source is the 28 November 1770 letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia; the 1767 citation was propagated by copying.

Voltaire’s French says “l’assurance est un état ridicule” — literally “certainty is a ridiculous state.” “Absurd” is Tallentyre’s 1919 word-choice, as noted on WIST; the meaning is faithful, but the popular English is a translation, not Voltaire’s literal phrasing.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are genuinely Voltaire’s, from an 1770 letter — only the date-and-recipient and the exact English word “absurd” are commonly gotten slightly wrong.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Voltaire wrote the line in 1770 while reacting to Baron d’Holbach’s Système de la nature, a sweeping work of materialist atheism. Voltaire — himself a fierce critic of the Church — found its confident denial of God as dogmatic as the faith it attacked.

The aphorism is his verdict on that kind of certainty: doubt is uncomfortable, but the person who claims to have settled the ultimate questions has simply stopped thinking. It became one of the most quoted expressions of Enlightenment skepticism.
